title_clean: Q&A: Mutual Fund vs Hedge Fund, REITs, Quitting Trading, F&O Mechanics
summary: Rapid-fire Q&A: REIT collateral limits, cost of rolling Bank Nifty futures for a year (~100 pt/month premium), why stock lending & borrowing loses to futures shorting, margin-adequacy math for 2-lot Nifty short, trading-ban MWPL thresholds, Bharat Bond volatility, correction-vs-crash definitions after Tesla's 21% day and $1T US tech wipeout.
lessons: Rolling long futures costs ~5-6% a year in premium; long-term positions belong in cash, shorts earn the premium.
Stock lending & borrowing loses to futures shorting: no futures premium, borrowing cost, and full option margin on the hedge.
Market-wide position limit above 95% bans a stock; the ban persists until it falls below 80% - even on expiry day.
Margin money is calibrated to cover ~99% of moves: 2 short Nifty lots lose only ~35-40K in a 500-point gap against 1L+ margin.
Corrections are -10 to -20%, bear territory beyond -20% - label drawdowns by definition, not by fear.

title_clean: Stock Recommendation: Power Finance Corporation (PFC) - Deep-Value PSU + Covered Calls

PFC profiled at ~₹90: P/E 3.31 (sector 21), P/B 0.37 (sector 1.81), >10% dividend yield (sector 0.85%), EPS ~₹27, government holds 56%. Government's own revenue need forces PSU dividend continuity - a structural, not cyclical, yield anchor.
Covered calls on a 10% yielder can stack to ~25-30%/yr: dividend + option income + modest appreciation.

title_clean: SEBI Multi-Cap Rejig: Why No Crash and No Smallcap Boom
summary: SEBI's 25/25/25 multi-cap mandate is skewered with a cake-fairness analogy: top-500 market cap is ~80% large, 15% mid, 5% small, so proportional allocation should be 80/15/5. ~₹40,000 cr must rotate out of large caps, but no Nifty crash or smallcap melt-up follows: money can exit to non-Nifty large caps, funds may reclassify or seek extensions; US-listed Indian ADRs stayed green.
lessons: Rules that ignore market-cap proportions create bureaucratic flows, not fundamental repricing - expected rebalance trades often fail to materialize.
Rebalance fear prices in the wrong sellers: mandate money can rotate within the large-cap universe rather than out of it.

summary: DXY primer: a 1973-vintage index of dollar strength vs six currencies (EUR 57.6%, JPY 13.6%, GBP 11.9%, CAD 9.1%, SEK 4.2%, CHF 3.6%), changed only once (DEM to EUR). lessons: The dollar index is a 50-year-old six-currency basket whose weights no longer match US trade - a good cue, not gospel.

title_clean: Carry Trade: Borrow Cheap, Invest High - and the Currency Trap
summary: Carry trade taught through a 1990s anecdote: borrow at 3% abroad, deposit at ~19.5% NRI rates in India - ₹10L became ₹25L in six years, netting ~₹13.75L. Risks: access and currency (1991's ~20% two-day devaluation). Foreigner's-eye math: Nifty 6,000→12,000 (2008-20) is 100% in rupees but ~10% in dollars at ₹40→₹75. Weak DXY = foreign tailwind.
lessons: FII returns are rupee returns discounted by currency: a 100% index gain can be ~10% in dollars if the rupee slides 40→75.
Carry profits die by devaluation, not by rates - always price the currency leg before the yield leg.
Weak dollar index = double benefit for foreign money (market return + currency); strong dollar = double whammy exit.

title_clean: Mazagon Dock IPO: Retail Allotment Rules and the Sell-Half-Keep-Half Wealth Rule
summary: IPO mechanics built on retail-rule tweaks: allotment now favors minimum applications, so apply minimum, at cutoff, via ASBA, on the last day, with multiple family applications. Mazagon Dock (1934 defence shipyard, 795 vessels incl. 25 warships, 3 submarines) at ₹135-145, lot 103, listing 12 Oct. Wealth rule: on a doubling, sell half to recover cost, hold the rest lifelong (Reliance Power ₹450→₹4 as the counter-example).
lessons: Retail IPO allotment favors minimum-bid applicants at cutoff - size beats wealth: many small applications win more than one big one.
ASBA keeps your money earning interest until allotment - never prepay an IPO.
The wealth rule: when an IPO doubles, sell half to recover cost and hold the rest for decades - one Infosys pays for nine dead issues.

Aggressive call selling against a falling stock positions cuts cost basis faster than averaging alone (ITC to ~171).

title_clean: Robinhood Traders: The Lockdown Newbie Wave and 30-Year Bear Markets
summary: The Robinhood phenomenon mapped to India: 300% jump in Zerodha's new demat accounts, 2.6M CDSL accounts since March (record 8,30,405 in June vs ~3L/month in FY20), retail at 68% of cash volumes - a decade high. Cautionary anchor: Nikkei 40,000 (1989) still ~half after 30 years; Shanghai never reclaimed its pre-Lehman 6,000 in 12 years; skills before size.
lessons: Record account openings mark euphoria tops more than opportunities - the wave that lifts markets also supplies its exits.
A market can stay below its high for decades (Nikkei 1989, Shanghai 2007) - 'it always comes back' is survivorship folklore.
Acquire skill before size: the lockdown cohort learned trading from YouTube tutorials with pandemic savings.

title_clean: TCS Buyback: Don't Chase the News - Sell the IV Spike
summary: TCS buyback at an all-time high puzzles everyone; SEBI's 75% promoter cap caps it at ~10% of public holding, making the rumoured ₹3,000 tender worth only ~₹25-30 per 10 shares - yet sentiment added 7.5%. The trade: IV jumped 33→39 (IV percentile 64→82), so a 2700 short straddle (lot 300) made ~₹4,000 in one session on ~₹1.5L effective margin, targeting IV crush after results.
lessons: Buyback news pops are sentiment, not value: capped tender sizes make the arithmetic trivial - fade the euphoria, don't chase it.
IV percentile above 80 after a news pop is the classic short-straddle entry; the target is post-event IV crush, not direction.
Event-day option income needs margin math: premium received offsets posted margin (₹2.09L posted → ~₹1.5L effective).
